accroche: In 1952, a 29-year-old architect cracks a script that had stayed silent for half a century.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1900, at the site of Knossos, on Crete, British archaeologist Arthur Evans unearths hundreds of clay tablets covered in unknown signs. He calls this script “Linear B,” as opposed to an older script, Linear A, which also remains undeciphered to this day. Evans is convinced that these tablets do not record Greek: the Minoan civilization, he thinks, predates the arrival of the Greeks on Crete. He dies in 1941 without having solved the mystery, and for half a century, no specialist manages to say what language these signs transcribe.

## An Architect, Not a Philologist

Michael Ventris is fourteen when he attends, in 1936, an exhibition where Arthur Evans, then 85, presents his Knossos discoveries to visiting schoolchildren. In his spare time, Ventris becomes one of the few amateurs to follow the case for sixteen years, all while pursuing a career as an architect, with no university training in linguistics.

The foundation on which he works comes from another self-taught student of the problem, the American Alice Kober, a professor of classics at Brooklyn College. Between 1943 and 1948, she methodically establishes that Linear B words vary by inflection (their endings change according to grammatical function), and builds a grid cross-referencing signs by their presumed consonant and vowel, without ever making a hypothesis about the language itself. Kober dies in 1950, at 43, without having completed the grid or identified the language.

## The Grid, Then the Greek Hypothesis

Ventris takes up Kober's grid and extends it. Against the prevailing view, which ruled out Greek, in spring 1952 he tests the hypothesis that the phonetic values obtained correspond to archaic Greek. The words begin to make sense. On July 1, 1952, in a broadcast on the BBC Third Programme, he announces his conclusion: the tablets of Knossos and Pylos are written in a difficult, archaic Greek, several centuries older than Homer. Philologist John Chadwick, who hears the broadcast, contacts him right away; he becomes the first specialist to validate the decipherment and the co-author of the scientific publication that follows, in 1953 in the *Journal of Hellenic Studies*.

## The Tablet That Settled It

The decisive proof comes from elsewhere. Archaeologist Carl Blegen, who is excavating Pylos, discovers several hundred new tablets in the summer of 1952. One of them, cataloged Ta 641, pairs each line of text with a drawing of a vessel. Without knowing these drawings in advance, Ventris applies his values to the signs: the line preceding a three-legged tripod reads *ti-ri-po-de*, literally “tripods.” The one preceding a vase with four handles reads *qe-to-ro-we*, “four-eared.” The text predicts exactly what the drawings show, without Ventris having been able to know it when he built his grid. It is this blind test, more than the announcement itself, that wins over the skeptics.

## What This Shifts

The episode shifts a conviction and repairs, in part, an oversight. The conviction: nothing required Mycenaean Greece to speak Greek several centuries before Homer; it was one hypothesis among others, set aside by most specialists, and it is the one that proved right. The oversight: the method that made the breakthrough possible was born with a little-known teacher, who died two years before seeing where her grid would lead.

repere.texte: Michael Ventris heard Arthur Evans present Linear B on a school visit in 1936, at age 14. He announces the decipherment sixteen years later, in a BBC broadcast aired on July 1, 1952, without any university training in linguistics.
repere.source: Faculty of Classics, University of Cambridge, “The Life of Michael Ventris”

carte.punch: A 29-year-old architect deciphered, in 1952, a script that philologists had judged impossible.
carte.idee: Arthur Evans discovers Linear B and believes it is not Greek. Michael Ventris, an amateur architect, takes up the grid of Alice Kober, who died in 1950, and tests the hypothesis that specialists had set aside: it is archaic Greek. A tablet from Pylos, describing tripods, confirms it blind.
carte.source_courte: Ventris & Chadwick, Journal of Hellenic Studies, 1953

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The details of the Pylos tablet that confirmed the decipherment.

quiz.question: What definitively convinced skeptical specialists that Ventris had indeed deciphered Linear B?
choix: The stance of John Chadwick, a respected philologist, who publicly validated Ventris's method
The comparison of Linear B with Linear A, which would have confirmed that they recorded the same language
A Pylos tablet where the text, read with Ventris's values, matched the vessel drawings accompanying it, without his having been able to foresee it
The discovery of a bilingual tablet, comparable to the Rosetta Stone, pairing Linear B with alphabetic Greek
quiz.explication: Pylos tablet Ta 641 pairs each line of text with a drawing of a vessel; applied blind, Ventris's values yield Greek words that match the drawings exactly (“tripods” in front of a tripod). Linear A remains undeciphered to this day, and no bilingual tablet of this kind exists for Linear B. It was a structural test, not a ready-made translation key, that won over the specialists.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Alice Kober establish between 1943 and 1948?
choix: That Linear B words vary by inflection
That the Knossos tablets recorded archaic Greek
That Linear A and Linear B record the same language
That Linear B signs come from the Phoenician alphabet
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kober showed that word endings change according to grammatical function, and built a grid cross-referencing signs by presumed consonant and vowel, without ever making a hypothesis about the language. It is this foundation that Ventris took up and extended.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was the Greek hypothesis set aside by most specialists?
choix: Because Linear A, which is older, had been read as non-Greek
Because Evans held the Minoans to predate the Greeks on Crete
Because no bilingual tablet had ever been found
Because the number of signs ruled out any European language
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Evans judged that Minoan civilization predated the arrival of the Greeks on Crete, so that its tablets could not record Greek, and his view prevailed for half a century. Linear A, for its part, has never been deciphered, to this day.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was John Chadwick's role?
choix: He introduced Ventris to Linear B at an exhibition
He gave Ventris the grid built at Brooklyn College
He discovered at Pylos the tablets that confirmed everything
He validated the decipherment and co-signed the 1953 publication
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Chadwick heard the BBC broadcast of July 1, 1952, and contacted Ventris right away. He became the first specialist to validate the decipherment, then co-author of the 1953 Journal of Hellenic Studies article.
